extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, policymakers, USPTO officials, legal economists, and patent policy practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether and how increasing patent examiner time allocations (and related Patent Office investments) improves patent quality, via an empirical cost–benefit analysis comparing ex ante examination to ex post litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient examiner time to conduct prior art search and articulate rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If examiners are not given enough time to evaluate applications, they may not be able to reject applications by identifying and articulating justifications with appropriate underlying legal validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent applications are presumptively valid on filing; an examiner who cannot conduct a sufficient search and articulate a proper basis of rejection during allotted review time is legally expected to allow the application. The article notes the average examiner spends only ~18 hours reviewing an application and documents how allocated hours fall with GS-level promotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant rate as an indicator of examiner time constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner grant rates increase as allocated examination time falls (e.g., an examiner promoted from GS-7 to GS-14 has a grant rate 13%–29% higher).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use grant rate changes across GS-level promotions as a measurable proxy for the influence of time constraints on outcome; regression specifications should include year, examiner experience, examiner fixed effects, technology-by-year fixed effects, and application controls to isolate time-allocation effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use EPO/JPO outcomes as an external benchmark of patent quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare U.S.-issued patents to outcomes at the European Patent Office and Japan Patent Office—offices that invest more resources per application but have similar patentability standards—to assess whether marginally issued U.S. patents are of questionable legal validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors find patents issued at higher GS-levels are less likely to be allowed by both the EPO and JPO, suggesting marginal U.S. issuances under time constraints are more likely invalid; this is an imperfect but informative benchmark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost–benefit framework: ex ante examination versus ex post litigation (rational ignorance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the social costs and benefits of investing more in ex ante administrative examination (increased examiner time) against relying on ex post litigation to police invalid patents, following Lemley’s 'rational ignorance' framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirically estimate the relationships Lemley assumed (e.g., how much invalid issuance falls with more time; how litigation costs change) rather than relying on assumed parameters; include private prosecution costs, licensing returns, and litigation costs in the comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate litigation savings from reducing invalid patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify potential savings in future litigation costs attributable to decreasing the issuance of invalid patents through enhanced examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parts II and the empirical exercises evaluate how increased examination time reduces litigation incidence/costs; include background on litigation expenses and causal links from time allocations to litigation savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate PTAB/post-grant savings from improved examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how augmenting examiner time allocations affects the frequency and cost of post-grant challenges (e.g., PTAB proceedings) and the associated savings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical investigation of the link between examination time allocations and PTAB savings is necessary to capture institutional shifts after the America Invents Act created new administrative challenge procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate prosecution savings to patent applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate changes in applicant prosecution expenses (interactions between applicants and the Patent Office) resulting from altered examiner time allocations and examination rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis should consider whether increased examiner time reduces the rounds of prosecution and applicant attorney time, and weigh any offsetting increases in attorney effort during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider other social savings from investing in ex ante examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for additional harms avoided by reducing invalid patents, such as crowding out of R&D, misallocation of resources, notice externalities, and downstream market harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although some of these effects are difficult to quantify, including them (conservatively) increases estimated net benefits; examples include reduced researcher time spent on litigation support and reduced negative spillovers to innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs of increasing Patent Office resources (hiring, salaries, opportunity costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the direct costs of augmenting examiner hours: hiring additional examiners, salaries, training, benefits, and the opportunity cost of diverting trained scientists/engineers from private sector R&D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate headcount needs (e.g., doubling examiners implies hiring ~8,000) and consider recruitment constraints and market wages; weigh these explicit costs against the estimated litigation and other savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional effects and incidence of financing
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze who bears the marginal costs and who receives benefits when choosing ex ante investment: patent applicants, patent holders, consumers, or taxpayers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider user fees versus general taxation to spread costs; account for potential pass-through of fees to customers and equity/efficiency implications of concentrated versus broad-based financing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target time increases toward higher GS-level examiners
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than uniformly increasing hours for all examiners, allocate larger time expansions to higher GS-level examiners because promotions currently reduce time and correlate with higher grant rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors propose increasing time allocations more heavily for senior examiners (e.g., GS-12 vs GS-11) to reduce heterogeneity in grant rates and improve equity of outcomes across applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsider aggressive scaling of time allocations upon promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Current practice reduces allocated hours roughly 10%–15% per GS promotion; this scaling may be too aggressive and induce inequitable outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust the rate at which time allocations decline with promotions to avoid large grant-rate increases tied to reduced time; empirical evidence suggests grant rates rise monotonically with GS-level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify fee schedule to eliminate financial incentives to grant patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust Patent Office fees and incentives that may create a pro-granting bias in examination outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior work (cited) argues fee structure can influence grant incentives; any fee changes should be studied for effects on filing volume and applicant behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase clarity of issued claims (procedural/format reforms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement reforms (e.g., claim templates, default dictionaries) to improve claim clarity and reduce downstream disputes over claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearer claims reduce uncertainty and potentially litigation; authors note this is complementary to time-allocation reforms but requires separate cost–benefit analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit continuations/repeat filings to reduce pro-granting bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict the number of times an applicant can refile the same application to mitigate tactics that exploit examination timing and encourage grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested as a reform to abolish pro-granting biases that arise from serial filings; cited literature argues for limits on continuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider elasticity of patent demand to fee increases
rubrics_metrics.description: When modeling fee-based financing of increased examiner resources, account for the price elasticity of patent filings—small fee increases may have negligible effects on filing volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite empirical literature indicating patent filing demand is relatively inelastic to small fee increases; therefore modest fee hikes may not reduce filings materially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for second-order effects on innovation and productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider potential broader economy effects such as scientists moving from private R&D to the Patent Office, and researcher time diverted to litigation, which may respectively decrease or increase innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These effects are theoretically ambiguous and difficult to quantify, but including them (where possible) refines welfare estimates; authors conservatively omit some due to estimation difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on empirical estimates rather than unsupported assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use novel data and rigorous empirical methods to estimate key parameters in the cost–benefit analysis (e.g., how much invalid issuance falls with more time), instead of assuming values as prior work did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors leverage 1.4 million applications and FOIA roster data plus quasi-experimental variation from GS-level promotions to obtain causal estimates; methodology and controls are specified to isolate time-allocation effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for time-sensitive bases of rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that some rejection reasons are more time-intensive (e.g., complex prior-art searches), and the relationship between time allocations and rejection activity will be stronger for these bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical tests should examine stronger relationships for time-sensitive rejection bases to validate that time constraints drive granting behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random assignment of applications within technology groups supports causal inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Because patent applications are randomly assigned to examiners within technology groups, variation in GS-level/time allocations can be exploited as plausibly exogenous for causal analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological designs should include fixed effects and controls to leverage this quasi-random assignment; the authors argue this institutional feature reduces selection bias concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of patentability as a legal constraint on outcomes under time pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Because applications are presumptively compliant on filing, if examiners lack time to search and justify rejections they are legally expected to allow the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any evaluation of time-allocation policies must account for this legal presumption (cited authority) that amplifies the effect of constrained examiner time on grant outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity objective: reduce heterogeneity of grant rates across examiners
rubrics_metrics.description: A policy goal is to create a more homogeneous pattern of grant rates across examiners so similar applicants receive similar Patent Office outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted time increases (especially for senior examiners) are proposed to reduce variance in grant rates and improve fairness across applicants who are randomly assigned.
